The regression line

Section titled “The regression line”

In months when the market rises 1%, how much does a certain stock rise on average? Here are 6 months of data: xxx is the market’s monthly return and yyy is the stock’s monthly return (%).

MonthMarket xxxStock yyy
1−4−4
2−2−3
3−1−0.5
412.5

Draw each month as a point. The points lie roughly along a line, but not exactly on it. Describing how the average of yyy changes with xxx by a line is called regression:

yi=a+b xi+eiy_i = a + b\,x_i + e_iyi​=a+bxi​+ei​

aaa is the intercept and bbb is the slope. y^i=a+b xi\hat y_i = a + b\,x_iy^​i​=a+bxi​ is the fitted value that the line gives at xix_ixi​; the actual value minus the fitted value, ei=yi−y^ie_i = y_i - \hat y_iei​=yi​−y^​i​, is the residual. The residual is positive when the point is above the line and negative when it is below. yyy is called the dependent variable and xxx the explanatory variable.

Ordinary least squares

Section titled “Ordinary least squares”

Infinitely many lines pass through these points. Which one should we choose? The most common rule is to make the sum of the squared residuals as small as possible:

min⁡a, b ∑i=1n(yi−a−b xi)2\min_{a,\,b}\ \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - a - b\,x_i)^2a,bmin​ i=1∑n​(yi​−a−bxi​)2

This is ordinary least squares (OLS). Squaring plays the same role as in the variance: positive and negative residuals do not cancel, and large deviations are penalized more. Solving this optimization problem (with the first-order conditions of 0.2 Optimization; the derivation is left as Exercises Question 5) gives

b=∑i(xi−xˉ)(yi−yˉ)∑i(xi−xˉ)2,a=yˉ−b xˉb = \frac{\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y)}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2}, \qquad a = \bar y - b\,\bar xb=∑i​(xi​−xˉ)2∑i​(xi​−xˉ)(yi​−yˉ​)​,a=yˉ​−bxˉ

The numerator and denominator of the slope are the sample covariance and the sample variance (both multiplied by n−1n - 1n−1), so bbb can also be written as Cov(x,y)Var(x)\frac{\text{Cov}(x, y)}{\text{Var}(x)}Var(x)Cov(x,y)​ (covariance). The second formula shows that the regression line always passes through the point (xˉ,yˉ)(\bar x, \bar y)(xˉ,yˉ​).

Example: in the table above, xˉ=0\bar x = 0xˉ=0 and yˉ=1\bar y = 1yˉ​=1.

The regression line is y^=1+1.5x\hat y = 1 + 1.5xy^​=1+1.5x. The 6 residuals are 1, −1, 0, 0, −1 and 1, and the sum of their squares is 4.

What the coefficients mean

Section titled “What the coefficients mean”

The number in front of the explanatory variable in a regression is a regression coefficient. The slope bbb means: when xxx rises by one unit, yyy changes by bbb units on average.

In the example, b=1.5b = 1.5b=1.5: for each percentage point of market return, the stock’s monthly return is 1.5 percentage points higher on average. The intercept a=1a = 1a=1: in months when the market return is 0, the stock returns 1% on average. In finance, the slope from regressing a stock’s return on the market return is the stock’s beta (beta), which 4.5 The Single-Index Model and Estimating Beta covers in detail.

Three things to keep in mind when reading a regression coefficient:

  • A coefficient has units, and its size depends on the units of xxx and yyy.
  • A coefficient describes an average relation, not one that holds every time: each point also has a residual.
  • The intercept is the fitted value at x=0x = 0x=0. If x=0x = 0x=0 is far outside the range of the data, the intercept itself may have no practical meaning.
Check C3

The intercept is the fitted value at which xxx? Are there observations near that xxx in the data?

Goodness of fit: R²

Section titled “Goodness of fit: R²”

How much of the variation in yyy does the line explain? Split the total variation of yyy into two parts:

∑i(yi−yˉ)2⏟SST=∑i(y^i−yˉ)2⏟ESS+∑iei2⏟SSR\underbrace{\sum_i (y_i - \bar y)^2}_{\text{SST}} = \underbrace{\sum_i (\hat y_i - \bar y)^2}_{\text{ESS}} + \underbrace{\sum_i e_i^2}_{\text{SSR}}SSTi∑​(yi​−yˉ​)2​​=ESSi∑​(y^​i​−yˉ​)2​​+SSRi∑​ei2​​​

SST is the total sum of squares, ESS the sum of squares explained by the regression, and SSR the sum of squared residuals. For the OLS line, this split always holds. The share of the total variation that the regression explains is R-squared (R2R^2R2):

R2=1−SSRSSTR^2 = 1 - \frac{\text{SSR}}{\text{SST}}R2=1−SSTSSR​

R2R^2R2 lies between 0 and 1. In the example, SST=25+16+2.25+2.25+4+49=98.5\text{SST} = 25 + 16 + 2.25 + 2.25 + 4 + 49 = 98.5SST=25+16+2.25+2.25+4+49=98.5 and SSR=4\text{SSR} = 4SSR=4, so R2=1−498.5≈0.96R^2 = 1 - \frac{4}{98.5} \approx 0.96R2=1−98.54​≈0.96: about 96% of the variation in the stock’s monthly return is explained by the variation in the market.

Check C4
In a regression, change the unit of yyy from percent to decimals (divide every yyy by 100), leaving xxx unchanged. R2R^2R2:
R2=1−SSRSSTR^2 = 1 - \frac{\text{SSR}}{\text{SST}}R2=1−SSTSSR​. When yyy is divided by 100, by what factor do SSR and SST change?
The sums of squares do shrink by a factor of 10,000, but R2R^2R2 is a ratio of two of them. Does the ratio change?
The residuals get smaller, but what about the total variation of yyy? What two things does R2R^2R2 compare?

How precise is a coefficient?

Section titled “How precise is a coefficient?”

Like the sample mean in 0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference, a regression coefficient is computed from one stretch of data and would be different with other data. The standard error of the slope is

SE(b)=se∑i(xi−xˉ)2,se=SSRn−2\text{SE}(b) = \frac{s_e}{\sqrt{\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2}}, \qquad s_e = \sqrt{\frac{\text{SSR}}{n - 2}}SE(b)=∑i​(xi​−xˉ)2​se​​,se​=n−2SSR​​

ses_ese​ is the standard deviation of the residuals. The divisor is n−2n - 2n−2 because two parameters, aaa and bbb, were estimated, so 2 degrees of freedom are lost (degrees of freedom).

In the example, se=4/4=1s_e = \sqrt{4 / 4} = 1se​=4/4​=1 and SE(b)=142≈0.154\text{SE}(b) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{42}} \approx 0.154SE(b)=42​1​≈0.154. The t-statistic (t-statistic) for testing whether the slope is 0 is

t=bSE(b)=1.50.154≈9.7t = \frac{b}{\text{SE}(b)} = \frac{1.5}{0.154} \approx 9.7t=SE(b)b​=0.1541.5​≈9.7

This is far above 1.96, so the slope is significantly different from 0. The 95% confidence interval for the slope is b±1.96×SE(b)b \pm 1.96 \times \text{SE}(b)b±1.96×SE(b), about [1.20,1.80][1.20, 1.80][1.20,1.80]. (With only 6 points, a critical value of the t distribution would strictly be more appropriate, and the interval would be wider; the numbers here are only a demonstration.)

Check C5
A regression slope is 1.2 with a standard error of 0.5, significantly different from 0 at the 5% level. This shows the slope has been estimated precisely.
Write down the 95% confidence interval of the slope and see how wide it is. What question does significance answer?

Omitted variable bias

Section titled “Omitted variable bias”

Suppose yyy is really determined by two variables:

y=α+β1x1+β2x2+εy = \alpha + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \varepsilony=α+β1​x1​+β2​x2​+ε

but only x1x_1x1​ is put into the regression. The coefficient of x1x_1x1​ then reflects more than the effect of x1x_1x1​ itself: if x2x_2x2​ is correlated with x1x_1x1​, part of the effect of x2x_2x2​ is attributed to x1x_1x1​. With a lot of data, the slope from regressing on x1x_1x1​ alone is close to

β1+β2⋅Cov(x1,x2)Var(x1)\beta_1 + \beta_2 \cdot \frac{\text{Cov}(x_1, x_2)}{\text{Var}(x_1)}β1​+β2​⋅Var(x1​)Cov(x1​,x2​)​

The extra second term is the omitted variable bias. It is non-zero only when two conditions both hold: the omitted variable really affects yyy (β2≠0\beta_2 \ne 0β2​=0), and it is correlated with the variable in the regression (Cov(x1,x2)≠0\text{Cov}(x_1, x_2) \ne 0Cov(x1​,x2​)=0).

Example: wages are regressed on years of education. People with more ability tend to get more education, and ability itself also raises wages. Ability is not in the regression, so the coefficient of education also picks up part of the effect of ability.

Check C6
In a city, regressing house prices on distance from the center gives a positive slope. The regression leaves out floor area: larger houses cost more, and houses further from the center tend to be larger. With floor area held the same, the true effect of distance on price:
The omitted area has a positive effect on price, and its covariance with distance is positive. What is the sign of the bias term β2CovVar\beta_2 \frac{\text{Cov}}{\text{Var}}β2​VarCov​? Does it push the regression slope up or down?
Which two conditions make the omitted variable bias nonzero? Do both hold here?
The question gives the sign of the effect of area on price and the direction in which area and distance move together. Those two signs decide the direction of the bias.

Correlation and causation

Section titled “Correlation and causation”

A significant regression coefficient only shows that two variables move together; it does not show that one causes the other. This is the difference between correlation and causation. A correlation may come from:

  • Reverse causation: yyy affects xxx, rather than xxx affecting yyy.
  • A common cause: a third variable affects both xxx and yyy. This is the omitted variable of the previous section.
  • Chance: when many variables are tested, some will be significant by luck (multiple testing).

To establish causation, you need evidence that rules out these possibilities, such as a randomized experiment, or a natural situation in which only xxx changes and everything else stays the same. Most regressions in investing (for example, estimating beta and factor exposures, 4.6 Multifactor Models) only need to describe how variables move together and do not need causation. But when a regression result is used to recommend “do xxx and you will get yyy”, the question of causation must be answered.

Check C7
Data show that households holding index funds have a much higher average net worth than those that do not. This shows that buying index funds makes households richer.
Did households get rich after buying funds, or buy funds after having money? Could something else affect both?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • Regression describes how the average of yyy changes with xxx by a line y^=a+bx\hat y = a + bxy^​=a+bx; a residual is the actual value minus the fitted value.
  • OLS minimizes the sum of squared residuals: b=∑(xi−xˉ)(yi−yˉ)∑(xi−xˉ)2b = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y)}{\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2}b=∑(xi​−xˉ)2∑(xi​−xˉ)(yi​−yˉ​)​, a=yˉ−bxˉa = \bar y - b\bar xa=yˉ​−bxˉ.
  • The slope is the average change in yyy when xxx rises by one unit, and it has units.
  • R2=1−SSRSSTR^2 = 1 - \frac{\text{SSR}}{\text{SST}}R2=1−SSTSSR​ is the share of the variation that the regression explains.
  • The standard error of the slope is se∑(xi−xˉ)2\frac{s_e}{\sqrt{\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2}}∑(xi​−xˉ)2​se​​; t-statistics and confidence intervals work as in 0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference.
  • Leaving out a variable that affects yyy and is correlated with xxx biases the coefficient. Correlation is not causation.
